Hugo Chávez. The Venezuelan military officer and politician who led a Bolivarian Revolution, transforming Venezuela into an anti-American, socialist-oriented state. He served as president for fourteen years and became a polarizing figure for his charismatic populism and radical redistributionist policies.

Chávez led a failed military coup in 1992, which earned him fame among Venezuela's poor. Released from prison, he ran for president and won in 1998. Once in power, he implemented the Bolivarian Revolution, a sweeping program of constitutional rewriting, wealth redistribution, and expanded state control of oil revenues. He used Venezuela's vast oil wealth to fund social programs in healthcare, education, and housing, and to provide regional aid to allied Latin American nations. In 2002, he survived a coup attempt and consolidated executive power by purging political opponents from the judiciary and military. He moved Venezuela toward authoritarianism through supermajority control of congress and manipulation of referenda. Dissidents were imprisoned and media outlets were shut down. Though he maintained mass support among the poor through charismatic leadership and populist rhetoric, he polarized the educated middle class. Chávez died in office in 2013. His successor Nicolás Maduro continued and radicalized his policies, leading to Venezuela's economic collapse.
